How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The data from Study 1 and Study 2 were also used to validate the misinformation exposure and policy-support measures reported in a separate paper (Cahill et al., under review). That paper reports the development and psychometric evaluation of these measures, whereas the present manuscript tests the substantive hypotheses preregistered for each study. There is no overlap in the hypotheses tested or analyses reported.

Introduction

Trans and gender diverse (TGD) people, those whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned to them at birth, experience disproportionately high rates of mental health difficulties, including anxiety, depression, and suicidality (Cahill et al., 2026; Jones et al., 2019). Prevalence is substantially higher than among cisgender populations (Hainey et al., 2025), with evidence indicating that these disparities are socially produced rather than reflecting inherent pathology among TGD people (Hoy-Ellis, 2023). Gender minority stress theory proposes that mental ill-health arises from the cumulative impact of minority stressors (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003), distinguishing distal stressors, such as experiences of discrimination and victimisation, from proximal stressors, such as expectations of rejection, identity concealment, and internalised stigma. The attitudes and behaviours of cisgender people are, therefore, an active social determinant of minority stress, and are shaped by a public information environment that is increasingly negative towards TGD people (Bracco et al., 2024; Connolly et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2020).

Negative discourses surrounding TGD people are especially acute in the United Kingdom (UK), where the legal, political and social position of TGD people has shifted markedly. Since 2025, the UK has fallen below the European average for LGBTQ+ rights protections, ranking 22 nd of 49 countries in the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map (ILGA-Europe, 2025). This decline has coincided with highly publicised developments affecting the rights and social position of TGD people, including the UK Supreme Court ruling in 2025 on the essentialist definition of sex under the Equality Act 2010, subsequent Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance published in 2026, and publication of the Cass Review in 2024. These developments have intensified debate about trans rights, within an information environment where anti-TGD claims circulate widely and often unchallenged, alongside a broader rise in populist and conspiratorial politics across Europe and North America.

Central to this environment is misinformation, defined here as false or misleading information that spreads, regardless of intent to deceive (Meade et al., 2024; The Alan Turing Institute, 2024). Misinformation is distinguished from simple error by being repeated, shared, and frequently politically motivated, accruing credibility through familiarity rather than evidence (Ludwig & Sommer, 2024). Anti-TGD misinformation frequently travels alongside two related belief systems: populism, a worldview pitting a virtuous ordinary people against a self-serving corrupt elite (Akkerman et al., 2014; Olivas Osuna et al., 2025), and conspiracy beliefs which attribute events to the secret, malevolent coordination of powerful groups (Jolley et al., 2025; van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018). These constructs are mutually reinforcing: populist and conspiratorial worldviews render misinformation more credible, and exposure to misinformation, particularly through social media, strengthens conspiratorial thinking (Chan et al., 2026; Enders et al., 2023). In the TGD context, this coalesces in narratives casting trans people and their allies as an organised "gender ideology" lobby pursuing hidden influence (Salvati et al., 2024, p. 301).

Both belief systems are associated with more hostile intergroup attitudes and reduced support for minority-protective policy, although the evidence is considerably stronger for conspiracy beliefs. Conspiracy beliefs about sexual and gender minorities predict prejudice and opposition to LGBTQ+ rights (Jolley et al., 2025; Salvati et al., 2024), and perceived minoritygroup status shapes which conspiratorial claims gain traction (Gundersen et al., 2023). Such narratives may be especially potent because they recast a minority seeking rights as a coordinated threat to the majority, licensing hostility while presenting it as self-defence (Ching, 2022; Jolley et al., 2025). These narratives have long been leveraged against LGBTQ+ people, such as during the AIDS crisis, where conspiracy theories about gay men proliferated (Heller, 2015). Populism's contribution is less certain. It may supply the people versus elite scaffolding onto which anti-TGD claims are hung (Paternotte & Kuhar, 2018), and populist attitudes are linked to exclusionary orientations toward outgroups (Olivas Osuna et al., 2025). However, only some forms of populism are associated with negative outgroup attitudes (Akkerman et al., 2017; Olivas Osuna et al., 2025), and populist antagonism is directed primarily upwards, at elites (Rooduijn et al., 2021). Whether populist beliefs are associated with prejudice towards TGD people therefore warrants scrutiny.

Within the UK, these belief systems attach to defined policy flashpoints, including single-sex spaces, competitive sport, NHS gender services to under-18s, and prison placement, where public attitudes are strongly shaped by gender-related beliefs (Connolly et al., 2025; Flores et al., 2016 Flores et al., , 2020). Yet direct evidence linking exposure to anti-TGD misinformation with prejudice and policy attitudes remains scarce, particularly within the UK. Connolly and colleagues (2025) position pervasive social and press media misinformation as a central driver of an increasingly hostile UK environment for TGD people. However, this link has been argued at the level of review rather than tested, individual-level relationships between misinformation exposure, prejudice, policy attitudes, and wellbeing unexamined. A further question concerns whether exposure translates into belief. Encountering a claim is not the same as accepting it, and repeated exposure may breed acceptance through familiarity or, for some, invite scepticism (Ludwig & Sommer, 2024). Because misinformation exposure has typically been inferred from broader belief systems rather than measured against the specific claims in circulation, whether agreement with those claims accounts for the link between exposure and attitudes remains untested.

These associations are unlikely to be uniform across cisgender individuals. Social media information literacy, the capacity to critically appraise online content, may weaken the link between exposure and belief (Heiss et al., 2023). Parasocial contact, the one-sided sense of connection formed with TGD media figures, extends the prejudice-reducing benefits of intergroup contact (Schiappa et al., 2005) and improves attitudes towards TGD people specifically (Chen & Zhang, 2022; Massey et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2020). Across two experiments, Jolley et al. (2025) demonstrated that cisgender people's positive parasocial contact with TGD creators on TikTok did not directly reduce trans conspiracy beliefs, but increased perspective-taking, which was in turn associated with lower conspiracy beliefs. In data pooled across three studies, more frequent positive contact with trans people showed the same indirect pathway. Jolley et al. (2025) found that parasocial contact with TGD creators reduced trans conspiracy beliefs indirectly, via perspective-taking, and note that such beliefs are related to, but distinct from, prejudice. Parasocial contact may therefore do more than lower conspiracy beliefs. Among those who hold them, familiarity with individual TGD people may weaken the extent to which beliefs about a coordinated trans lobby translate into negative evaluations and policy opposition.

TGD people are also directly affected by this information environment. Within gender minority stress theory, a public discourse saturated with hostile and inaccurate claims can be understood as a distal stressor in its own right, becoming a chronic, ambient signal of societal rejection that need not take the form of a discrete interpersonal event to be harmful (Hendricks & Testa, 2012). Unlike interpersonal discrimination, which is episodic, a hostile media climate is continuous and difficult to escape, reaching even those who are otherwise insulated from face-to-face prejudice (Meyer, 2003; Pang et al., 2022). This exposure may bear on two facets of TGD wellbeing in particular: mental health and the sense of being recognised in one's gender. Frequent encounters with anti-TGD misinformation may, therefore, be associated with poorer mental health, including heightened anxiety and depression (Wall et al., 2026). Further, exposure to negative TGD media has been associated with reduced access to gender affirming care in Sweden (Indremo et al., 2022). Such exposure may also erode social gender-role recognition, the sense that one's gender is recognised and affirmed by others (Jones et al., under review), an aspect of gender congruence closely tied to wellbeing (Jones, Bowe, et al., 2023; Jones et al., 2018). This is because public questioning of whether trans identities are legitimate targets precisely the external affirmation on which recognition depends.

Coping with these harms is often buffered by social connectedness with others who share similar lived experiences (Frost & Meyer, 2012; Jones et al., 2026; Puckett et al., 2025).

In response to stigma and exclusion, TGD people may withdraw from social groups and environments perceived as unsafe. While such withdrawal can protect against immediate harm, it may also limit access to social support. For example, TGD young people who distance themselves from unsupportive family frequently report unmet emotional and practical support needs (Jones et al., 2024). Similarly, avoiding hostile physical activity environments can reduce opportunities for social connection, identity affirmation, and wellbeing (Jones et al., 2017). By contrast, connections with other TGD and LGBTQ+ people can foster belonging, social support, and collective efficacy, promoting resilience (Jones et al., 2026). Disengagement from TGD community spaces, including online spaces where hostile content circulates may therefore be double-edged, reducing exposure to harmful content while limiting opportunities for connection and collective support.

The Current Research

Research on misinformation and on gender minority stress has developed largely in parallel. The first has examined how misinformation, conspiracy beliefs and populism shape intergroup attitudes and policy preferences (Jolley et al., 2025; Olivas Osuna et al., 2025; Salvati et al., 2024). The second has examined how hostile social environments affect the wellbeing of minoritised groups (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003; Puckett et al., 2025).

To our knowledge, no research has examined anti-TGD misinformation among cisgender and TGD people concurrently, nor has UK research measured exposure to the specific claims currently in circulation, as distinct from endorsement of broader conspiracy or gender-ideology beliefs.

The present research addresses both pathways across two concurrent quantitative studies, advancing a dual-pathway account in which anti-TGD misinformation may harm TGD communities indirectly, by degrading the surrounding attitudinal climate, and directly, by acting as a minority stressor. Both studies draw on a set of contemporary, UK-specific misinformation and policy-support measures developed for this programme through community-engaged focus groups and a ranking survey (Cahill et al., under review).

Study 1 assesses whether cisgender people's exposure to anti-TGD misinformation is associated with less positive attitudes towards TGD people and lower support for transinclusive policiesfoot_0 , whether these associations operate through conspiracy beliefs and populist attitudes, whether agreement with the misinformation statements accounts for these associations, and whether they are moderated by social media information literacy and parasocial contact. Study 1 hypotheses are as follows:  H1: Greater anti-TGD misinformation exposure will be associated with (a) less positive attitudes and (b) lower policy support.

 H2: These associations will be mediated by (a) trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (b) populist attitudes, such that greater exposure will be associated with stronger beliefs, which will in turn be associated with less positive attitudes and lower policy support.

 H3: Social media information literacy will moderate the association between anti-TGD misinformation exposure and (a) trans-specific conspiracy beliefs and (b) populist attitudes, such that the positive associations will be weaker among those with higher literacy.

 H4: Parasocial contact with TGD people will moderate the association between transspecific conspiracy beliefs and (a) attitudes and (b) policy support, such that the negative associations will be weaker among those with greater parasocial contact.

 H5: Anti-TGD misinformation exposure will be indirectly associated with (a) less positive attitudes and (b) lower policy support via agreement with the misinformation statements, tested in a model estimated separately from H2.

Study 2 turns to TGD people, examining whether misinformation exposure functions as a minority stressor associated with greater mental distress and reduced social gender-role recognition, and whether TGD community engagement and disengagement moderate these relationships. We control for participants' experiences of trans-negativity (gender-based discrimination, victimisation and microaggressions), to test whether misinformation exposure is associated with these outcomes over and above them.

We make the following hypotheses for Study 2:  H1: Greater anti-TGD misinformation exposure will be associated with (a) higher mental distress and (b) lower social gender-role recognition, controlling for experienced trans-negativity.

 H2: TGD community engagement will moderate these associations, such that the adverse association between misinformation exposure and (a) mental distress and (b) social gender-role recognition will be weaker at higher levels of engagement.

 H3: TGD community disengagement will moderate these associations. Given competing theoretical predictions, we do not specify a direction.

Study 1

Method Study 1's design, sampling procedure, hypotheses and analysis plan were preregistered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MRQ4H). We make no deviations from our analysis plan, bar the shift in sampling approach mentioned below. All accompanying documents for this project, including our open materials, anonymised data and R code, can be found on the OSF: https://osf.io/wznvu/overview.

Participants and Design

We employed an online cross-sectional survey hosted on Qualtrics and recruited via Prolific. Our final sample comprised 400 participants who self-identified as cisgender people from the UK, aged 18 to 75 (M age = 39.2, SD age = 12.6). Table 1 displays the sample composition.

The sample was predominantly White (87%) and based in England. During data collection we monitored the political composition of the accruing sample and, observing a skew toward leftleaning participants, introduced party-based quotas. This was not specified in our preregistration. Prolific offers pre-screeners for party affiliation but not left-right orientation. We made this adjustment to better reflect the current UK political landscape. Adjustments were based solely on political demographics and the research team remained blind to responses on all substantive measures throughout. The resulting sample sat just left of centre (M = 2.84, SD = .99). A priori power analyses were conducted using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis calculator for indirect effects (Schoemann et al., 2017), and G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) for the moderation effects. Assuming standardised paths of β = .20, N = 400 provided power of .95 for both parallel indirect effects. For interactions, assuming f² = .02, and power = .80, N = 395 was required, making moderation the binding constraint.

Nottingham Trent University's Research Ethics Committee granted ethical clearance.

Propagating the very misinformation we sought to study posed a clear ethical risk. To mitigate this, participants in both studies were presented at debrief with a corrective document that directly refuted each misinformation statement used (see the OSF).

Measures

After providing informed consent and demographic details, participants completed the measures described below. Both the presentation order of the measures and the order of items within each measure were randomised across participants. Full details of all measures are available in the open materials on the OSF. organised group of trans people works for more power, hiding behind the demand for more rights"). Items not naming a target group were unchanged. Items are rated from 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating stronger conspiracy beliefs.

Trans Attitudes and Beliefs Scale

Trans Attitudes and Beliefs Scale replaced by "British" following prior UK research (Olivas Osuna et al., 2025; e.g., "the politicians in the British parliament need to follow the will of the people"), rated from 1 to 5.

Populist Attitudes Scale (Akkerman et al., 2014): comprises 8-items, with "Dutch"

Higher scores indicate greater populist beliefs.

Social Media Information Literacy Appraisal Subscale (Heiss et al., 2023):

is the 4item subscale, which asks how easy participants find tasks such as "critically reviewing post content for accuracy", rated from 1 (difficult) to 7 (easy). Higher scores indicate a greater selfperceived ability to appraise social media information.

TGD Parasocial Contact: was measured with a bespoke 4-item measure of the frequency (e.g., "how often do you watch, follow, or engage with content featuring trans and gender diverse people on social media?") and quality (e.g., "when engaging with trans and gender diverse content, I enjoy it") of contact through media and online platforms, each rated from 1 to 5. The two quality items were shown only to participants scoring two or more on either frequency item, so the six participants reporting no contact were scored on the frequency items alone. Higher mean scores indicated greater TGD parasocial contact.

TGD Misinformation Exposure:

This bespoke measure assesses the frequency with which participants encounter common forms of TGD-related misinformation in the media and public discussion. The statements were developed in a previous stage of this research (see Cahill et al., under review). Participants rate how often they have encountered each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) never encountered to ( 5 strongly disagree to ( 5) strongly agree (e.g., "trans people should be able to access single-sex spaces and services that align with their gender identity"). Higher scores indicate greater support for trans-inclusive policies. This was used as one of our two outcome variables.

Statistical Analyses

All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.6.0). All continuous predictor, mediator, moderator, and outcome variables were standardised prior to analysis, and reported coefficients are standardised betas. We tested our hypotheses using structural equation modelling in the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012). Residual covariances were estimated between the two mediators and between the two outcomes. Models were estimated using maximum likelihood, with full information maximum likelihood (FIML) used to handle missing data so that all available data were retained. Indirect effects were tested using the product-of-coefficients approach, with percentile 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals based on 5000 resamples; an indirect effect was considered present where the confidence interval did not contain zero (Yzerbyt et al., 2018). The moderating roles of social media information literacy and parasocial TGD contact were tested via standardised interaction terms. We controlled for age (in years), political orientation (left-right), and education (as a continuous variable). For transparency, the pattern of findings was unchanged with and without these covariates.

We additionally tested an indirect effect of misinformation exposure via agreement with the misinformation statements in a separately estimated model. Because agreement with antitrans misinformation and the attitudes outcome are conceptually proximate, we first examined their bivariate correlation as a discriminant-validity check. We pre-specified that a very high correlation (r ≥ .80) would indicate that the two may not be empirically distinct constructs, in which case we would interpret the corresponding mediation with appropriate caution and foreground this limitation.

Results

Preliminary Analyses

Given the potential correlation between the predictor variables, moderator and mediator variables, we assessed and determined that the variance inflation factor was acceptable (VIF < 2). We also assessed univariate normality, which we deemed acceptable as skew and kurtosis were all within ±2.

Table 2 displays the descriptive statistics and internal consistency for each variable.

The TABS showed excellent reliability, as did the Trans-Specific Conspiracy Beliefs Scale and the Social Media Information Literacy appraisal subscale. The Populist Attitudes Scale was the weakest performer, though still acceptable. Encouragingly, the bespoke measures developed for this research cohered well: misinformation exposure, misinformation agreement, policy support, and parasocial contact all demonstrated good internal consistency. Descriptively, participants reported relatively positive attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people but below the midpoint support for trans-inclusive policies. Reported exposure to and agreement with misinformation were both around the scale midpoint, as was parasocial contact.

Conspiracy beliefs were comparatively low, while populist attitudes sat above the midpoint. Notes. Square brackets represent the 95% CI. Means (M) and standard deviation (SD), should be interpreted on each variable's response scale. All measures except for TGD attitudes and media literacy (on a 1-7 scale) were responded to on a 1-5 scale.

Table 3 displays the correlations between each variable. Agreement with misinformation was very strongly associated with both attitudes (r = -.82) and policy support (r = -.78) and was closely linked to conspiracy beliefs (r = .81). Given the strong correlations between agreement and the outcome variable (attitudes), and the fact it shows strong conceptual overlap with conspiracy theories, this additional analysis should be interpreted with caution.

Primary Analyses

We first assessed the model fit against our pre-registered criteria (CFI ≥ .95, TLI ≥ .95, RMSEA ≤ .06, with 90% CI upper bound ≤ .08, and SRMR ≤ .08). Two indices indicated excellent fit (CFI = .98; SRMR = .02) and two fell short of our pre-registered cutoffs (TLI = .90; RMSEA = .08, 90% CI [.06, .11]). The TLI fell only marginally short, and the RMSEA is known to over-reject correctly specified models at low degrees of freedom, as here (df = 10; Kenny et al., 2015). The SRMR, which is not subject to this penalty, indicated excellent fit, as did the standardised residuals (all ≤ .06, bar one at -.16). Most modification indices suggested atheoretical reverse paths. The exception, and the source of the largest residual, was the unmodelled association between parasocial contact and conspiracy beliefs. We did not add this path, as contact was pre-registered as a moderator of the mediator-outcome paths rather than as a predictor of the mediators, and adding it would have been a data-driven departure from the pre-registered model. As such, we deemed the model to appropriately represent the data. Figure 1 provides an overview of the relationships in the model.

The following results relate to our pre-registered hypotheses. Misinformation exposure was significantly and positively associated with both proposed mediators: conspiracy beliefs, β = .22, 95% CI [.14, .31], p < .001, and populist attitudes, β = .15, 95% CI [.05, .24], p = .002.

Conspiracy beliefs were, in turn, significantly and negatively associated with both attitudes towards trans and gender diverse people, β = -.45, 95% CI [-.54, -.35], p < .001, and policy support, β = -.28, 95% CI [-.38, -.18], p < .001. Populist attitudes, however, predicted neither attitudes, β = -.03, 95% CI [-.10, .05], p = .484, nor policy support, β = .04, 95% CI [-.04, .11], p = .333.

Consistent with this pattern, the indirect effect of misinformation exposure through conspiracy beliefs was significant for both attitudes, β = -.10, 95% CI [-.15, -.06], and policy support, β = -.06, 95% CI [-.10, -.03]. The indirect effects through populist attitudes were nonsignificant for both outcomes (attitudes β = -.004, 95% CI [-.02, .01]; policy β = .005, 95% CI [-.01, .02]). Regarding the direct effects, misinformation exposure was not significantly associated with attitudes in the full model, β = -.04, 95% CI [-.10, .03], p = .247, but was significantly, if modestly, associated with policy support, β = -.08, 95% CI [-.15, -.002], p = .042. When looking at the bivariate relationships between misinformation exposure and each outcome while only controlling for the covariates, there was a significant relationship with both outcomes (attitudes β = -.12, 95% CI [-.20, -.04], p = .003; policy β = -.11, 95% CI [-.19, -.03], p = .006). The relationship between exposure and both outcomes therefore operated substantially through conspiracy beliefs rather than populist attitudes.

Neither of the pre-registered moderation hypotheses was supported. The misinformation exposure by media literacy interaction was not significantly associated with conspiracy beliefs, β = -.03, 95% CI [-.10, .05], p = .433, or populist attitudes, β = .03, 95% CI [-.06, .13], p = .523. Similarly, the conspiracy beliefs by parasocial contact interaction was not associated with attitudes, β = .04, 95% CI [-.03, .11], p = .248, or policy support, β = -.05, 95% CI [-.14, .04], p = .347, and the populism by parasocial contact interaction was also nonsignificant for both outcomes (attitudes β = -.04, p = .349; policy β = -.003, p = .933).

The following observations were not pre-registered and are reported as exploratory.

Study 1 Discussion

Study 1 examined whether cisgender people's exposure to anti-TGD misinformation was associated with attitudes towards TGD people and support for trans-inclusive policies, and whether these associations operated through conspiracy beliefs and populist attitudes. Greater misinformation exposure was associated with stronger conspiracy beliefs and stronger populist attitudes. However, only conspiracy beliefs were associated with more negative attitudes and lower policy support. The indirect effects through conspiracy beliefs were significant for both outcomes, while those through populist attitudes were not. In an additional analysis, agreement with the misinformation statements fully accounted for the association between exposure and both outcomes. Neither social media information literacy nor parasocial contact moderated the hypothesised pathways. However, parasocial contact was directly associated with more positive attitudes and greater policy support.

A key finding was that the direct associations between exposure and the two outcomes (attitudes towards TGD people and policy support) were largely explained by the mediators.

The direct association with attitudes became non-significant, and the direct association with policy support remained significant but small, the latter suggesting exposure may also shape policy preferences through routes not captured here. Importantly, this was driven entirely by conspiracy beliefs, with no indirect association through populist attitudes for either outcome.

This difference between the two mediators may partly reflect how the two constructs were measured. The Trans-Specific Conspiracy Beliefs Scale frames TGD people as an organised group pursuing hidden influence, whereas the Populist Attitudes Scale makes no reference to TGD people. Conceptually, conspiracy beliefs also tend to be directed at specific groups (van Prooijen & van Vugt, 2018), whereas populist attitudes are directed primarily at elites and may not reliably extend to hostility towards outgroups (Rooduijn et al., 2021). This is consistent with the weaker evidence base for populism noted earlier and suggests populism may reflect a general antagonistic framing rather than one directed at TGD people specifically.

Encountering TGD misinformation was not, in itself, strongly related to TGD attitudes.

Instead, acceptance of those claims was central, such that agreement with the misinformation statements accounted for the association between exposure and both outcomes. This is consistent with the illusory truth effect, whereby repeated exposure to a claim increases its perceived credibility (Fazio et al., 2015; Hasher et al., 1977), and with evidence linking frequent exposure to misinformation to greater belief (e.g., Udry & Barber, 2023). It is therefore acceptance of the claims, rather than the encounter itself, that appears to matter for how people evaluate TGD people (Ludwig & Sommer, 2024). However, agreement correlated at -.82 with attitudes and .81 with conspiracy beliefs, and whether it represents a distinct construct or a further indicator of a single evaluative orientation remains unclear. The same may apply to the conspiracy beliefs measure itself, which could partly capture this broader orientation rather than a separate set of beliefs.

Neither moderation hypothesis was supported. Media literacy has been proposed as a protective resource against misinformation (Guess et al., 2018 (Guess et al., , 2020) ) with interventions reliably improving people's ability to distinguish accurate from inaccurate information; however, their effects on subsequent attitudes are smaller and less consistent (Droog et al., 2026). As media literacy was self-reported here, the null finding may partly reflect a gap between perceived and actual ability to identify misinformation. Alternatively, participants better able to recognise misinformation may have been no less likely to hold the beliefs it supports, particularly where those beliefs aligned with existing political commitments (Van Bavel et al., 2024).

Parasocial contact showed a substantial direct association with both outcomes but did not buffer the path from conspiracy beliefs to either outcome. We had reasoned that familiarity with individual TGD people might weaken the extent to which conspiracy beliefs translate into negative evaluations. However, Jolley et al. (2025) found that parasocial contact with TGD creators did not directly reduce conspiracy beliefs, but increased perspective-taking, which was in turn associated with lower conspiracy beliefs. This positions contact as operating on those beliefs rather than on their consequences. Our results are broadly consistent with that account.

Contact was also associated with lower conspiracy beliefs in the present sample (r = -.41), consistent with the pooled association reported by Jolley and colleagues. As perspective-taking was not measured here, whether it accounts for the association between parasocial contact and the outcomes remains a question for future research. However, given the cross-sectional design, it is equally plausible that people with more positive attitudes towards TGD people are more likely to seek out TGD creators in the first place.

Study 2

Method Study 2's design, sampling procedure, hypotheses and analysis plan were preregistered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/W79AU). We make no major deviations from our analysis plan, but document changes to how the latent factors and covariances were modelled below. All accompanying documents for this project, including our open materials, anonymised data and R code, can be found on the OSF: https://osf.io/wznvu/overview.

Participants and Design

We employed an online cross-sectional survey hosted on Qualtrics and recruited via Prolific. Our final sample comprised 290 participants who self-identified as trans or gender diverse from the UK, who were aged 18 to 58 (M age = 28.1, SD age = 7.7). Table 4 displays the sample composition. The sample was predominantly White (88.6%) and based in England. The sample also predominantly fell to the left, or very left, of the political spectrum (87.6%). In terms of gender-affirming care, the largest group of participants reported that they were "not pursuing medical transition" (38.6%), followed by those "currently undergoing medical transition" (30.7%), those "seeking medical transition but have not yet accessed it" (18.3%), and those who had "completed all the medical transition steps" they wish to pursue (11.0%).

Most of the sample reported being able to live in their affirmed gender day-to-day, either fully (43.8%) or in some contexts but not others (51.7%). A priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) or the moderation effects, the binding constraint in this design, indicated that N = 279 was required to detect the smallest effect size of interest (f² = .035) with α = .05 and power = .80. Although recruitment slowed before our target of 300, the final sample exceeded this requirement. The design was therefore powered to detect small-to-moderate interaction effects; smaller interactions may not be reliably detected.

Measures

We used the same demographic questions and procedures as Study 1. The open materials for this study are also available on the OSF. We used the same TGD misinformation exposure measure as Study 1, as well as the following measures. The order of the measures and the order of the items within each measure were randomised.

Social Gender Role Recognition (GCLS; Jones et al., 2018):

is a 4-item subscale of the Gender Congruence and Life Satisfaction Scale which assesses the extent to which a person feels their gender is recognised and affirmed by others (e.g., "I have felt comfortable with how others have perceived my gender"), rated from 1 (never) to 5 (always).

Mental Distress: was indicated by the GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006) and the PHQ-9 (Kroenke et al., 2001), which assess anxiety and depressive symptoms respectively over the previous two weeks (e.g., "Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge"; "Little interest or pleasure in doing things"). Both are rated from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day). Scores of ≥ 8 and no) and summed. We made two wording changes for affirming language and UK relevance: "gender reassignment" became "gender transition", and the reference to the DMV became "at the hospital or GP".

Statistical Analyses

Our analysis approach followed Study 1, with two differences. First, two constructs were modelled as latent factors rather than observed composites: mental distress, indicated by PHQ-9 and GAD-7 total scores, and experienced trans-negativity, indicated by GIMS total scores and a combined GMSR discrimination and victimisation score. Because the loadings of each two-indicator factor were constrained to unity, we report unstandardised coefficients as the primary estimates, alongside fully standardised coefficients for comparability. Second, the pre-registration specified a covariance between misinformation exposure and trans-negativity and a residual covariance between the two outcomes but did not address covariances between trans-negativity and the remaining exogenous variables. We therefore allowed trans-negativity to covary with all other exogenous variables. Age and experienced trans-negativity were included as covariates.

Results

Preliminary Analyses

First, we assessed and determined that the variance inflation factor was acceptable (VIF < 2). We also assessed univariate normality, which we deemed acceptable as skew and kurtosis were all within ±2.

Descriptively, misinformation exposure scores fell slightly above the scale midpoint (M = 3.65, SD = .89; possible range 1-5). Mean scores on both mental health measures exceeded the clinical thresholds for depressive symptoms (M = 11.14, SD = 6.57) and for anxiety symptoms (M = 9.22, SD = 5.61). In total, 57.2% of participants scored at or above the threshold for clinically relevant depressive symptoms and 57.9% for clinically relevant anxiety symptoms.

Table 5 displays the internal consistency and correlations for each variable. In this table, we include the composite of the latent factors for trans-negativity (comprised of microaggressions and overt discrimination and victimisation) and mental distress (comprised of PHQ-9 and GAD-7) that are used in the subsequent primary models, rather than the individual scales themselves. Internal consistency was generally good to excellent across each of the measures used. However, internal consistency for community disengagement was poorer. As such, any coefficients relating to community disengagement, including the interaction term, should be interpreted cautiously.

Primary Analyses

The pre-registered model, in which the loadings of both two-indicator latent factors were freely estimated, fitted the data poorly (CFI = .92, TLI = .85, RMSEA = .08, 90% CI [.06, .10], SRMR = .07) and produced a large number of inadmissible bootstrap solutions (1,703 of 5,000), reflecting the instability of latent factors with only two indicators.

We therefore made two changes. First, we constrained the loadings within each latent factor to equality (i.e., both fixed to 1), a common approach to stabilising two-indicator factors. Second, we allowed the latent trans-negativity factor to covary with all other predictors in the model (community engagement and disengagement, their interaction terms, and age). The findings from both models remained consistent. Model fit was assessed against the same pre-registered criteria as Study 1 and showed the same pattern. CFI (.97) and SRMR (.03) indicated excellent fit, while TLI (.91) and RMSEA (.07, 90% CI [.04, .09]) fell below our cutoffs. As in Study 1, the two shortfalls were on indices sensitive to model size and parsimony, whereas the SRMR, which carries no such penalty, indicated excellent fit. Standardised residuals were all ≤ .07 except two involving social gender-role recognition, and the modification indices suggested only a pair of equal and opposite residual covariances between the trans-negativity indicators and social gender-role recognition, for which we had no theoretical justification. We therefore retained the model (see Figure 2).

The following results relate to our pre-registered hypotheses. Consistent with H1a, greater exposure to TGD-related misinformation was significantly and positively associated with mental distress, b = 0.13, 95% CI [0.02, 0.24], β = .14, p = .024, controlling for experienced trans-negativity. H1b was not supported: exposure was not significantly associated with social gender role recognition, b = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.09], β = -.02, p = .689.

Neither of the pre-registered moderation hypotheses was supported. Contrary to H2, the misinformation exposure by community engagement interaction was not significantly associated with mental distress, b = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.11], p = .803, or with social gender role recognition, b = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.04], p = .162. Similarly, and with no direction specified a priori, the exposure by community disengagement interaction was not significantly associated with mental distress, b = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.17, 0.03], p = .175, nor with social gender role recognition, b = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.21], p = .091. Neither community engagement nor community disengagement therefore buffered or amplified the association between misinformation exposure and either outcome.

The following observations were not pre-registered and are reported as exploratory.

Community engagement was associated with lower mental distress, b = -.13, 95% CI [-.26, -.02], β = -.15, p = .035. Community disengagement was associated with greater social gender role recognition, b = .21, 95% CI [.08, .34], β = .21, p = .002, though given its lower internal consistency this should be interpreted cautiously. Experienced trans-negativity was strongly associated with both greater mental distress, b = .58, 95% CI [.39, .80], β = .48, p < .001, and lower social gender role recognition, b = -.38, 95% CI [-.64, -.16], β = -.28, p = .002. Study 2 Discussion

Study 2 examined whether exposure to anti-TGD misinformation was associated with mental distress and reduced social gender-role recognition for TGD people themselves, and whether community engagement or disengagement moderated these associations. Greater misinformation exposure was associated with higher mental distress but was unrelated to social gender-role recognition. Experienced trans-negativity, by contrast, was associated with lower social gender-role recognition. Neither community engagement nor disengagement moderated these associations. Levels of mental distress were high, with 57.2% and 57.9% of participants scoring above the clinical thresholds for depressive and anxiety symptoms, respectively (i.e., PHQ-9 ≥ 10; GAD-7 ≥ 8).

The association between misinformation exposure and mental distress remained significant when experiences of discrimination, victimisation and microaggressions were controlled for, suggesting that anti-TGD misinformation may represent an aspect of minority stress not fully accounted for by experienced trans-negativity. This is consistent with treating a hostile information environment as a distal stressor, rather than as a proxy for interpersonal mistreatment (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003).

Unexpectedly, anti-TGD misinformation exposure was unrelated to social gender-role recognition, which we anticipated would be particularly vulnerable to public questioning of the legitimacy of TGD identities (Jones et al., under review). Whether a person's gender is recognised by others may relate more to interpersonal relationships or transition-related circumstances than to national discourse. This may explain why trans-negativity, which is encountered interpersonally, was associated with lower social gender-role recognition, whereas misinformation exposure was not. If so, environmental stressors of this kind may bear on generalised distress while leaving identity-specific appraisals relatively untouched, a distinction worth pursuing in future minority stress research.

Neither moderation hypothesis was supported. The absence of buffering by community engagement is surprising, given consistent benefits of community connectedness for TGD wellbeing (Frost & Meyer, 2012; Puckett et al., 2025). However, while these direct benefits are well established (Mezza et al., 2024; Valentine & Shipherd, 2018), evidence that connection buffers the effects of minority stressors is less consistent (Mezza et al., 2024). Our findings mirror this pattern as engagement was directly associated with lower distress, but it did not buffer the association between misinformation exposure and distress. That said, the present study may have been underpowered to identify modest buffering effects.

A further possibility concerns how community engagement relates to the stressor itself.

Minority stress theory proposes that community resources attenuate stress by allowing members to reappraise stigma collectively as a feature of society rather than of themselves (Meyer, 2003). This may be less effective when the community is also a route through which the stressor is encountered. Interpersonal discrimination is experienced individually and can be met with collective support, whereas a hostile information climate reaches the whole community, so those to whom TGD individuals turn face the same stressors (Wall et al., 2026).

Consistent with this, exposure was positively associated with engagement in our sample, perhaps because community spaces also circulate, discuss and contest anti-TGD content.

Where engagement involves repeated discussion of hostile claims, it may itself become a stressor (Meyer, 2003). This does not in itself explain the absence of an interaction, but suggests that engagement may operate as a channel of exposure as well as a source of support. Exposure was also positively associated with disengagement, consistent with disengagement being a response to hostile content rather than simply the opposite of engagement.

This distinction has implications for how the buffering hypothesis is specified. Minority stress theory does not generally distinguish between community resources as sources of support and as sources of exposure. Our findings suggest that this distinction may matter (see also Cahill et al., 2026). Community connection demonstrates consistent benefits (Mezza et al., 2024; Valentine & Shipherd, 2018), but may have little purchase on a stressor that reaches the community through the same networks that provide support.

The disengagement findings warrant caution. Internal consistency for this subscale was poor (ω = .65), so the null interactions may reflect a genuine absence of moderation or attenuation due to measurement error. In exploratory analyses, disengagement was directly associated with greater social gender-role recognition, but not with distress. Whether withdrawal from a hostile discourse shields TGD people or isolates them remains open, and addressing it will require a more reliable measure.

Importantly, only 16.2% of the Study 2 sample were trans women, despite trans women being the principal subject of anti-trans narratives in the UK (Bracco et al., 2024; Connolly et al., 2025). Three of the four policy areas identified through our item development, single-sex spaces, participation in competitive sport and prison placement, are most often associated with trans women (Connolly et al., 2025; Jones et al., 2017). Trans women were similarly underrepresented (9.7%) in our previous national UK sample (Cahill et al., 2026). This may nonetheless limit generalisability, as experiences of minority stress could vary across gender groups with trans women experiencing higher levels of some forms of trans-negativity (Evje et al., 2024). Future research should deliberately oversample trans women, and, where sample size permits, examine whether these associations differ across TGD identities given minority stress exposure is not evenly distributed (Hainey et al., 2025; Rimes et al., 2019).

General Discussion

Across two concurrent studies, we examined whether exposure to anti-TGD misinformation that specifically relates to TGD people was associated with cisgender people's attitudes towards TGD people and support for trans-inclusive policies (Study 1), and whether it was associated with mental distress and social gender role recognition for TGD people themselves (in Study 2). Among cisgender participants, greater exposure was associated with less positive attitudes and lower support for trans-inclusive policies, and these associations operated largely through trans-specific conspiracy beliefs rather than through populist attitudes.

Among TGD participants, greater exposure was associated with higher mental distress, over and above experiences of gender-based discrimination, victimisation and microaggressions, though it was not associated with social gender-role recognition. Both arms of the dual pathway we proposed therefore received some support, albeit asymmetrically.

The direct association between misinformation exposure and both outcomes in Study 1 was largely explained by conspiracy beliefs and, in a separate model, by agreement with the misinformation statements once those variables were accounted for. In Study 2, misinformation exposure was associated with mental distress after controlling for trans-negativity. The same information environment may, therefore, operate through two distinct mechanisms depending on people's identities. For cisgender people it functions persuasively, with harm arising through what is believed; for TGD people it functions as an ambient stressor, with harm arising through what is encountered. This is consistent with evidence that restrictive anti-TGD legislation is associated with poorer mental health among TGD people irrespective of individual endorsement (Lee et al., 2024).

As such, interventions addressing the two are unlikely to be the same. Established approaches to countering misinformation, including debunking and fact-checking, psychological inoculation or prebunking, accuracy prompts, and media literacy training, all operate primarily on how information is received and evaluated (Droog et al., 2026; Kozyreva et al., 2024). Each targets the pathway identified in Study 1 and based on our findings such approaches may be well placed to protect the attitudinal climate surrounding TGD people.

None of them, however, reduces the volume of TGD misinformation content in circulation, which is the feature of the environment that Study 2 suggests matters for TGD people themselves. Protecting TGD wellbeing would, therefore, require either changes to the information environment itself or forms of support that help people live within an environment that is unlikely to change. This is a demanding prospect given evidence that anti-TGD misinformation is increasing (Billard, 2023 (Billard, , 2024;; Connolly et al., 2025) and recent changes by key social media companies that have loosened content moderation, including of hateful content (e.g., Paul et al., 2025). It also identifies a gap in that the intervention literature is largely organised around belief, while one of the two harms we document does not run through belief at all but rather simple exposure.

A further observation spanning both studies was the absence of moderation: neither social media information literacy nor parasocial contact moderated the hypothesised associations in Study 1, and neither community engagement nor disengagement moderated either association in Study 2. For community engagement in particular, this replicates our previous findings. In a national sample of 5856 TGD young people in the UK, access to

LGBTQ+ affirming spaces and perceived community acceptance were consistently and independently associated with better mental health, yet showed no evidence of buffering gender minority stressors (Cahill et al., 2026). That study attributed the null partly to the reduced variability of binary moderator indicators, but the present study used continuous measures and reached the same conclusion. Taken together, these findings suggest that community-level resources may operate additively rather than conditionally, contrary to one of the central predictions of minority stress theory (Hendricks & Testa, 2012; Meyer, 2003).

We would not read this as evidence that buffering does not occur. Interaction effects demand considerably more power than main effects, cross-sectional designs are poorly suited to capturing processes that unfold over time, and our study examined only two of many possible community resources. What our findings do suggest is that the additive benefits of affirming environments should not be assumed to extend to conditional protection against a hostile public discourse, and that buffering hypotheses may need to be specified with reference to the kind of stressor involved.

The role of political orientation also warrants comment. It was the strongest single association in the Study 1 model, exceeding that of misinformation exposure itself, and our Study 2 sample was predominantly left-leaning. It is therefore difficult to establish how far misinformation exposure operates independently of prior ideological commitments.

Participants already holding more conservative positions may encounter, attend to and accept these claims more readily, consistent with accounts of politically motivated reasoning (Van Bavel et al., 2024). Our design prevents us from distinguishing between these possibilities, and we advise against interpreting our findings as evidence that exposure exerts influence independently of the political commitments that shape it.

Limitations and Directions for Future Research

Several limitations should be considered. Most importantly, both studies were crosssectional, and the direction of the associations we report cannot be established. It is equally plausible that participants holding more negative attitudes towards TGD people sought out, attended to and recalled more TGD-related misinformation. The very strong association between agreement with the misinformation statements and attitudes is consistent with this limitation. In Study 2, participants experiencing greater distress may have been more vigilant towards, or more likely to recall, hostile content. Cross-sectional designs are also poorly suited to detecting buffering, since such effects may reflect processes unfolding over time (Meyer, 2003).

Several measurement limitations also apply. Exposure was self-reported, and recognition of a claim may be inflated by familiarity with it, particularly among those who already agree with it. Study 2 also did not measure proximal processes, such as appraisals of the misinformation encountered or expectations of rejection, through which exposure may be associated with distress. In addition to the poor internal consistency for the community disengagement subscale, the misinformation items developed for this project were intended to capture claims circulating in the UK at the time of data collection (2026) and are, by design, time limited. Our sample was also predominantly White and based in England which limits the generalisability of the findings.

Future research should use longitudinal or diary designs to establish the temporal ordering of exposure, distress and community engagement, as these would also be better placed to detect buffering. A broader range of potential moderators should also be examined. Among cisgender samples, experimental designs manipulating exposure could establish whether exposure shapes conspiracy beliefs and attitudes, and, given the direct associations observed for parasocial contact in Study 1, contact-based interventions warrant evaluation alongside belief-focused approaches.

Conclusion

In conclusion, anti-TGD misinformation was associated with harm along two pathways.

Among cisgender people, exposure was associated with less positive attitudes towards TGD people and lower support for trans-inclusive policies, largely through acceptance of the claims themselves, particularly when those claims were conspiratorial. Among TGD people, exposure was associated with greater mental distress, consistent with misinformation acting as a minority stressor. None of the protective factors we examined weakened either pathway, although parasocial contact with TGD people was beneficial in its own right. Tackling the first pathway is likely to need interventions that address both belief and contact, whereas tackling the second will mean attending to the information environment itself and to how TGD people can be supported within it.

This was used as our predictor variable.TGD Misinformation Agreement:Using the same set of statements as the TGD Misinformation Exposure measure, this measure assesses the extent to which participants endorse each claim (seeCahill et al., under review). Participants indicate how much they agree or disagree with each statement on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) strongly disagree to (5) strongly agree. Higher scores indicate greater agreement. This was used as a mediator variable in a confirmatory mediation model estimated separately from the conspiracy-belief and populism mediation (H5). TGD Policy Support: This bespoke measure assesses support for trans-inclusive policy positions across four areas which we developed in an earlier research stage (see Cahill et al., under review). Each policy issue is presented as a directional statement keyed toward the transinclusive position, and participants indicate their agreement on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) .27, .42], p < .001, and policy support, β = .31, 95% CI [.22, .40], p < .001, such that greater contact was associated with warmer attitudes and stronger policy support.

[

Political orientation was also a notable variable across the model, most strikingly for conspiracy beliefs, β = .51, 95% CI [.42, .59], p < .001, with more right-leaning participants reporting stronger conspiracy endorsement. Education was negatively associated with both mediators (conspiracy b = -.10, p < .001; populism b = -.14, p < .001). Hypothesis five was tested in a separate model. Misinformation exposure was significantly and positively associated with agreement with the misinformation statements, β = .22, 95% CI [.14, .30], p < .001. Agreement was, in turn, strongly and negatively associated with both attitudes towards TGD people, β = -.74, 95% CI [-.83, -.66], p < .001, and TGD policy support, β = -.67, 95% CI [-.76, -.59], p < .001. The indirect effect of exposure was significant for both attitudes, β = -.16, 95% CI [-.23, -.10], and policy support, β = -.15, 95% CI [-.21, -.10]. Neither direct effect was significant once agreement was accounted for, indicating that the association between exposure and each outcome was carried entirely by the indirect path via agreement.

Multidimensional Transgender and Nonbinary Resilience Scale (MTNRS; Puckett et al., 2025): measures TGD-specific resilience across four subscales. For the present study, we used the Community and Societal Engagement (CSE; 8 items; e.g., "Engaging with TNB communities online or in person helps me get through hard times") and Community and Societal Disengagement (CSD; 4 items; e.g., "Disconnecting from anti-trans media helps me deal with hardships") subscales. Participants respond on a 5-point scale and higher scores indicate greater community and societal engagement and disengagement, respectively. Experienced Trans-Negativity: was indicated by two measures. From the Gender Minority Stress and Resilience Measure (GMSR; Testa et al., 2015) we combined the victimisation (6 items; e.g., "I have been pushed, shoved, hit, or had something thrown at me because of my gender identity or expression") and discrimination (5 items; e.g., "Because of my gender identity or expression, I have had difficulty finding a bathroom to use when I am out in public") subscales, which assess lifetime experiences. Each item is answered on a fourcategory scale (never; yes, before age 18; yes, after age 18; yes, in the past year), collapsed to binary (0 = never,1 = any endorsement) and summed.
